cases.abstract: Conformal prediction controls whether a prediction set contains the target, but many applications require control of graded errors rather than a binary failure event. Conformal risk control calibrates a nested prediction family to bound the expected loss on a new observation at a prescribed level alpha. The procedure adds a worst-case contribution for the unseen observation to the calibration loss before selecting a parameter. For exchangeable, bounded, right-continuous loss functions that decrease with the parameter and admit a safe endpoint, this correction yields a finite-sample guarantee averaged over calibration and test data. Under independent, identically distributed nonnegative losses with no jumps at any fixed parameter value, the expected risk lies within 2B/(n+1) below alpha, where B bounds the loss; this gap is sharp in general. A counterexample shows that boundedness alone is insufficient without monotonicity. Experiments on segmentation, multilabel classification, hierarchical classification, and question answering produce mean risks close to their targets across 1,000 random splits. Extensions address further risk functionals and specified distribution shifts. The contribution expands what can be calibrated while identifying the structural assumptions required for valid control.
cases.methods: Let R_n(lambda) be the mean calibration loss over n observations and B a known upper bound on every loss. The calibration rule selects the smallest lambda for which [n R_n(lambda) + B]/(n+1) is at most alpha, reverting to the safe maximal parameter if no such value exists. The added B reserves enough loss for one unobserved test case, rather than treating calibration performance as population risk. To justify the rule, compare it with an infeasible parameter chosen using all n+1 losses. The corrected rule is at least as large as this symmetric choice, so non-increasing losses cannot be worse. Exchangeability makes the held-out loss average to the full-sample loss conditional on the unordered collection, and right-continuity ensures the threshold is attained. This argument controls expected loss jointly over calibration and test randomness, not loss for every observation.
cases.results: Across 1,000 random splits, polyp segmentation and MS COCO yield mean false-negative risks of 0.0987 and 0.0996 against a target of 0.1, with between-split standard deviations of 0.0114 and 0.0052. These observations support near-target average control, not a claim that every split stays below the target. The two tasks also use different calibration sizes, 1,000 and 4,000, so their differing dispersion does not isolate an application effect. Hierarchical ImageNet classification gives a mean normalized distance loss of 0.0499 at a target of 0.05 while usually retaining leaf-level predictions, suggesting that control need not force uniformly coarse outputs. The theoretical counterexample supplies the consequential adverse result: for a non-monotone bounded loss, the same calibration rule can produce expected risk arbitrarily close to B. Replacing each loss by its supremum over larger parameter values restores control, but may sacrifice usefulness when non-monotonicity is substantial.
cases.notes: Numerical summaries describe variation across random splits. The central guarantee averages calibration and test randomness. The question-answering candidate threshold has the opposite direction to the main theorem's parameterization, so that formula is not reproduced. No extension is interpreted as automatic validity under an unknown shift.

cases.abstract: Distribution shifts can invalidate prediction sets even when the underlying model and calibration scores are repeatedly updated. Adaptive conformal inference responds by updating the nominal miscoverage parameter after each revealed outcome, lowering it following a miss and raising it following coverage. This feedback calibrates the quantile argument rather than specifying a model of the shift. With suitable quantile conventions and a positive fixed step size, the realized miscoverage frequency converges to the target for any data-generating sequence. That long-run guarantee does not certify coverage at each time. Stronger concentration and mean squared marginal miscoverage bounds are established under a stationary hidden Markov setting with fixed score and quantile functions, linking performance to environmental dependence and changes in the optimal calibration parameter. Volatility forecasting and county-level election prediction illustrate improved local coverage relative to holding the nominal parameter fixed. However, removing volatility normalization from the conformity score produces substantially larger coverage swings even with adaptation. The findings identify both the reach of error feedback and its limits: local performance depends on score design and the adaptation rate, and the procedure requires an outcome to be revealed at each step.
cases.methods: At time t, the method forms a prediction set by thresholding the current conformity score at the estimated quantile indexed by 1-alpha_t. After observing the response, it records err_t as one for a miss and zero otherwise, then applies alpha_{t+1} = alpha_t + gamma(alpha-err_t), with gamma > 0. A miss therefore enlarges subsequent sets by decreasing the nominal miscoverage parameter; a covered response moves it in the opposite direction. Quantile conventions outside the unit interval allow the whole response space or an empty set, keeping the parameter bounded even though it is not clipped to [0,1]. Summing the updates makes cumulative deviation from target miscoverage proportional to the difference between the initial and final parameters. Boundedness consequently limits absolute frequency deviation to (max{alpha_1,1-alpha_1}+gamma)/(gamma T), yielding convergence without a distributional model for the observations.
cases.results: In volatility forecasting, adaptation keeps 500-day local coverage near the 90% target while a fixed nominal parameter shows pronounced departures, including undercoverage for Fannie Mae during the 2008 crisis. Both procedures use rolling GARCH forecasts and score calibration based on 1,250 trading days, so the comparison tests feedback beyond recent-data refitting. The four displayed stocks were selected for clear fixed-calibration failures among twelve examined, although adaptive coverage was favorable across all twelve. Score choice nevertheless changes the result: using unnormalized absolute residuals causes much wider coverage swings than scaling residuals by predicted volatility. This contrast shows that feedback does not remove the need to stabilize the score distribution. In the election experiment, counties are ordered by time zone and randomized within each zone, rather than following actual reporting times. Adaptive calibration keeps 300-county local coverage approximately at 90%, whereas fixed calibration dips around zone transitions. These descriptive comparisons support local adaptation in the tested sequences, separately from the unconditional long-run frequency guarantee.
cases.notes: The long-run guarantee concerns empirical frequency, not timewise coverage or interval efficiency. Stronger local theory assumes stationarity of the joint environment-parameter process and fixed score and quantile functions; it does not automatically cover rolling refits in the experiments. The financial plots are selected failure cases, and the election ordering approximates geographic reporting drift rather than replaying election night. No interval-width improvement is claimed.
